newsitem.title: ITALY: Milan soccer club seeks listing in 1999 - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Milan soccer club seeks listing in 1999 - newspaper.

text.p: Italian soccer champions AC Milan are planning a stock flotation in 1999 by which time they hope money will be flowing into club coffers from pay-per-view television, an Italian newspaper reported on Wednesday.
"Investors don't look at the past but at the future, at your chances of increasing revenues," Milan's vice president Adriano Galliani told Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera in an interview.
The club, which is being advised by investment bankers Rothschilds and by Lehman Brothers, was aiming for a listing on the London stock exchange, the newspaper reported.
Galliani said AC Milan was attracted to London because it was the stock exchange with most experience of handling soccer club flotations.
A number of British clubs, among them Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur, have been listed on the London market in recent years.
Manchester United was the British club which could be most closely compared to Milan, Galliani said.
The Manchester club, which like Milan has an international following, joined the stock market more than five years ago and is now valued at more than 400 million pounds.
Galliani said Milan's annual turnover was 130 billion lire ($77.2 million), higher than Manchester United, whose sales he estimated at 120 billion a year, the Corriere reported.
"The fundamental difference is in costs, which they manage to rationalise better than us," he said.

"On the basis of these considerations, Milan does not believe that it is an advantage to arrive first on the stock exchange. The important thing is to arrive prepared when the market is more mature," he said.
A number of Italian clubs, including Lazio and Juventus, are considering flotations. The London market is an attractive option because of perceived less arduous listing requirements.
The Milan Stock Exchange requires a new company to show profits for three consecutive years before listing, but most top Italian soccer clubs have been run at a loss in recent years.
Milan is counting on an increase in income from per-per-view television which is expected to take off when a new contract regulating television rights comes into force in July 1999.
Sponsorship contracts with sportswear maker Lotto and car manufacturer Opel also fall due for renewal in 1999.

Milan currently receives 12 billion lire a year from the Lotto deal and 10.4 billion from Opel, the newspaper reported, adding that the club would hold out for more money when the contracts were renegotiated.

The club is still pondering whether to acquire the San Siro grounds it currently rents jointly from the city council with local rival Internazionale or whether to build its own stadium on a greenfield site.
"San Siro has an enormous attraction but we have not yet quantified the cost of transforming it into an equipped commercial centre," Galliani told the newspaper.

Galliani said Manchester's Old Trafford stadium, which Milan sees as a model to be emulated, was set to gross revenues equivalent to more than 30 billion lire this season. $=1,688 lire ($ = 1684 Italian Lire)
